Dermatology · published research

Herpes zoster

A small randomized pilot found faster healing when near-infrared LED was added to antiviral care for acute ophthalmic zoster, while pain differences were not statistically significant. Small controlled and uncontrolled reports also address postherpetic neuralgia, and prevention findings are mainly observational.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A small randomized pilot found faster healing when near-infrared LED was added to antiviral care for acute ophthalmic zoster, while pain differences were not statistically significant. Small controlled and uncontrolled reports also address postherpetic neuralgia, and prevention findings are mainly observational.

Summary of the Evidence

The category contains 19 publications: 17 human reports, one review, and one editorial. Most address postherpetic neuralgia rather than active shingles. Human reports include three randomized trials, ten non-randomized studies, three case reports, and one case series. One publication reports both a 63-person series and a 12-person crossover component. A 1979 herpetic-stomatitis report has unclear zoster specificity.

Human and clinical evidence

A randomized pilot enrolled 28 Korean patients with acute ophthalmic zoster. Both groups received famciclovir; one also received 830-nm LED on days 0, 4, 7, and 10. Mean healing time was 13.14 days with LED and antiviral care versus 15.92 days with antiviral care alone. Pain improved numerically more with LED, but the difference was not statistically significant (Park et al. 2013).

For postherpetic neuralgia, a double-blind crossover study of 20 people reported reduced pain intensity and distribution after 830-nm treatment compared with sham. A separate placebo-controlled crossover study included only eight participants and compared two power settings with sham near the stellate ganglion. These small older trials provide controlled observations but do not establish the size or durability of benefit (Moore et al. 1988 Hashimoto et al. 1997).

Other reports include single-arm series and a 250-person retrospective study associating earlier treatment with less postherpetic neuralgia. Without a control group, this cannot show prevention. Improvement in a 15-person single-arm pilot cannot separate treatment from time or co-care.

Animal evidence

No animal study was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No zoster-specific cell or ex-vivo study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Clinical protocols include 830-nm near-infrared LED or diode laser, 633-nm red visible light, and 904-nm near-infrared light. The acute pilot used four visits over ten days but did not report every dose detail. PHN protocols vary in device, power, site, and session count. An eight-person study compared 60 and 150 mW but does not establish a general dose rule. Acute infection and chronic nerve pain require separate interpretation.

Interpretation

A small acute-disease pilot found faster healing without a statistically significant pain difference. Small PHN trials reported pain reductions, while prevention evidence is mainly observational. These findings do not establish a general treatment effect for herpes zoster.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for pain reduction in postherpetic neuralgia Low for faster healing in acute herpes zoster Very low for preventing postherpetic neuralgia
Publications and records19 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Small controlled studies report pain changes in postherpetic neuralgia and one 28-person pilot found faster lesion healing during acute zoster, but these are separate outcomes and settings. Prevention evidence is mainly retrospective and cannot show that early light treatment caused fewer later cases. Larger masked trials should separately test acute healing, persistent neuralgia, and prevention with longer follow-up.
